sections.content: On the evening of 24 June 2026, at around 18:04 local time (2204/2205 UTC), two major earthquakes struck north-central Venezuela about 39-40 seconds apart: a magnitude 7.2 foreshock near San Felipe, Yaracuy (depth about 22 km) and a magnitude 7.5 mainshock near Yumare, Veroes, Yaracuy (depth about 10 km, shallow), with epicentres also described as some 28-30 km north-west of Montalbán, Carabobo, and west of Caracas near Yaracuy and Carabobo (OCHA, PAHO/WHO). USGS recorded this as the strongest earthquake in Venezuela in more than 125 years, generating very strong to violent shaking (peak intensity approaching MMI 9) felt across a densely populated corridor including Caracas, La Guaira, Miranda, Carabobo, Aragua, Falcón and Yaracuy, and as far as Colombia (Data Friendly Space/USGS/Al Jazeera). The shocks occurred on the Boconó-Morón-El Pilar fault system at the Caribbean-South American plate boundary; USGS issued a Red PAGER alert indicating high probable casualties and extensive damage, and a brief Caribbean tsunami advisory was cancelled within about an hour.

The primary hazard was the dual shallow earthquake sequence (M7.2 and M7.5), followed by extensive aftershock activity: at least 20 aftershocks within two hours of the mainshock (six felt in Caracas), more than 302 aftershocks by 26 June (OCHA), nearly 1,000 by 6 July (UNFPA), and over 1,000 by mid-July, including a M5.1 event near Tucacas (Falcón) on 25 June and a M4.4 aftershock near Guatire (Miranda) on 26 June; USGS estimated about a 40% chance of a magnitude 6+ aftershock in the first week. The Shelter Cluster/UNHCR flagged secondary hazard risk from the onset of the annual rainy season, with potential for heavy rains, hurricanes or tropical low-pressure systems triggering landslides and mud flows in already seismically weakened slopes, requiring landslide and debris-flow mapping in the North Coastal Range. PAHO also identified elevated risk of outbreaks of vaccine-preventable diseases (measles, diphtheria, pertussis, polio), acute diarrheal disease, cholera, and other water/vector-borne illnesses linked to displacement, overcrowding and damaged WASH systems.

UNDP's RAPIDA assessment estimated 8.6 million people exposed to above-moderate shaking across northern Venezuela, including about 2.1 million exposed to stronger shaking, with 1.7 million structures located in affected areas. The earthquake struck a context of protracted economic and humanitarian crisis: Venezuela ranked 24th of 97 crises on the INFORM Severity Index (high severity, 7.6/10) as of May 2026, with nearly 8 million people already in humanitarian need before the quakes (IRC/UNDRR). ACAPS and REACH note widespread pre-existing vulnerabilities in the hardest-hit states (La Guaira, Caracas, Carabobo, Yaracuy, Aragua, Falcón): weak shelter, water and health systems, substandard and unreinforced construction with poor enforcement of building codes, informal settlements on unstable hillsides, a 94% poverty rate and 46% multidimensional poverty rate in La Guaira, 62% of housing in fragile condition with repair needs, and a Protection Cluster that had reached only 8% of its 1.9 million target population by April 2026. About 30% of the population is under 18 and 9% over 65 (IFRC), and years of emigration (roughly 8 million people) left critical workforce gaps affecting search-and-rescue and recovery capacity (IRC).

Casualty figures rose steadily and sometimes diverged between sources: Data Friendly Space reported 164 dead/971 injured on 25 June (up from an initial 32 dead); OCHA Sitrep No.3 (26 June) reported a provisional 920 dead/3,360 injured and REACH the same day cited 589 dead/2,980 injured; by 29 June MSF reported 1,430 dead/3,230 injured while UNHCR cited 1,719 dead, 5,034 hospitalised and 15,866 affected; IFRC's 1 July brief noted "tens of thousands" reported missing, with USGS modelling giving even odds that final deaths fall between 1,000-10,000 and a 30% chance of exceeding 10,000; UNFPA (6 July) reported 3,342 dead/16,470 injured, rising to 4,490 dead by UNICEF's 15 July count and 5,208 dead per CESVI by 20 July, with people injured holding at 16,740 across PAHO, UNFPA and CESVI reports from early July onward. Displacement estimates also varied: OCHA cited over 3,000 displaced (26 June), UNHCR 15,000+ affected/displaced by 29 June, UNFPA 17,345 who lost homes and 10,702 in 79 temporary camps by 6 July, rising to 17,907 homeless per UNICEF (15 July) and CESVI (20 July). Infrastructure damage reports progressed from 1,423 affected structures (OCHA, 26 June) to 2,501 damaged sites including 774 housing units, 189 fully collapsed, and 38 hospitals (UNHCR, 29 June), with CESVI (20 July) citing 856 affected buildings; UNDP estimated preliminary direct physical damage at US$6.7 billion (about 6% of GDP) within hours of the quake, while UNDRR's 3 July analytical estimate put total direct damage at approximately US$37 billion (US$24 billion to buildings, US$13 billion to infrastructure), equivalent to roughly 3-4% of exposed stock. Key infrastructure losses included closure of Maiquetía/Simón Bolívar International Airport, suspension of Caracas Metro and railways, multi-state power outages, and damage to electricity, water, telecommunications, roads and bridges.

Documents report significant prevention gaps rather than successful mitigation measures: ACAPS states that most buildings in Venezuela are unlikely to have been built in line with modern earthquake regulations, citing reports of a lack of enforcement of building standards (CNN, APnews). IFRC and ACAPS both note widespread informal settlements built on unstable hillsides and vulnerable unreinforced construction as pre-existing risk factors that amplified damage. No risk-financing, retrofitting programmes, or land-use planning measures prior to the event are described in the documents.

The documents do not describe specific pre-event early warning systems, contingency plans, drills or stockpiles for this earthquake; FUNVISIS (Venezuela's seismological institute) is referenced only as an information source, not for prior monitoring performance. A brief Caribbean tsunami advisory was issued by relevant authorities and cancelled within about an hour, indicating some monitoring capacity was operational at the time of the event (Data Friendly Space, citing USGS/CNN/NPR). Pre-existing weak institutional capacity is implied by ACAPS' observation that censorship and limited transparency have historically weakened public trust in official information, likely hindering situational awareness and risk communication during the response.

The Venezuelan government declared a national state of emergency and designated La Guaira a disaster zone; Acting President Delcy Rodríguez and National Assembly President Jorge Rodríguez provided official casualty updates from 25-26 June. The Venezuelan Red Cross began search-and-rescue in the Capital District on 24 June and received CHF 2 million from IFRC's DREF on 25 June; IFRC launched a CHF 50 million Emergency Appeal on 26 June (later CHF 55 million Federation-wide) targeting 300,000 people, and set up a field hospital at Jorge García Carmeiro Stadium plus a Field Operations Centre. International UNDAC and USAR teams under INSARAG coordination arrived from 25 June; authorities imposed temporary access restrictions to La Guaira state from the night of 26 June to prioritize search and rescue. The Expanded Health Cluster, co-led with the Ministry of Popular Power for Health (MPPS), was activated 26 June to consolidate a single response mechanism integrating state actors, UN agencies and NGOs. UN agencies scaled up: UNICEF, UNFPA (targeting 64,000-230,000 people for SRH/GBV services), UNHCR (seeking $14.8-14.85 million for 30,000 people), WFP-supported logistics, and PAHO/WHO delivered medical supplies and equipment, including to Maternal and Child Hospital Leopoldo Aguerrevere by mid-August. NGOs including MSF, Good Neighbors, CESVI, Project HOPE/Proyecto Esperanza and the Turkish Red Crescent mobilized emergency relief, health posts and needs assessments. Constraints included blocked roads from debris, damaged Maiquetía airport, disrupted telecommunications, erratic fuel availability, and logistics congestion at the airport and Port of La Guaira, as flagged by UNICEF and the OCHA Logistics Working Group ($0.8M requirement).

By late July, CESVI reported the response transitioning from immediate emergency to a more structured, large-scale operation, and by 12 August (PAHO Sitrep No.9, seven weeks on) efforts were shifting toward early recovery, including rehabilitation planning at priority health facilities, restoration of intensive care and maternity capacity at Hospital Dr. José Gregorio Hernández, and a USD 18 million PAHO Revolving Fund credit line to support national vaccine supply security. OCHA's Humanitarian Response Plan Addendum (July 2026) and UNICEF's HAC Appeal Addendum ($65.7 million to reach 470,000 people, including 167,000 children) outline sector plans aligned with the earthquake addendum targeting 1.3 million affected people across 7 states. IRC warned on 22 July that without urgent investment in local economies and livelihoods, Venezuela risked spiraling into a deeper crisis, citing UNDRR's $37 billion damage estimate and noting that over half the population already lived in extreme poverty before the quakes.

The Health Cluster (27 June) identified critical gaps in food, safe water, hygiene kits, non-food items, clothing and safe temporary shelter, alongside needs for logistics support, specialized medical personnel, mental health/psychosocial support, and protection pathways for unaccompanied children. REACH highlighted pre-existing weak shelter, WASH and health systems in Aragua, La Guaira, Carabobo and Falcón limiting absorptive capacity, with water cited as the top priority need nationally since March 2026. Project HOPE's assessment (16 health facilities, 48 hours post-event; expanded to 12 facilities/160 households) found significant gaps in emergency obstetric care, mental health and psychosocial support, water quality monitoring, handwashing infrastructure and protection mechanisms. UNFPA flagged unmet needs in survivor-centred GBV and SRH services amid overcrowded shelters and family separation. PAHO (10 July) noted persistent gaps in registration and follow-up of injured and hospitalized patients, likely causing underestimation of casualties, plus a severely strained health system with shortages of personnel, medicines, supplies and surgical capacity even before the quakes.

ACAPS noted that censorship, limited transparency and restrictions on media and civil society have weakened public trust in official information, increasing reliance on informal networks and complicating coordination between authorities, responders and communities, delaying assistance delivery and targeting. The Shelter Cluster/UNHCR Environmental Quick Note recommended guiding the response with Sphere Shelter Standard 7 and ECHO Minimum Environmental Requirements, including environmental impact assessment, sustainable materials, debris reuse/recycling, safe solid waste management and protection of ecological value at temporary settlement sites, alongside daily monitoring of rainfall/landslide risk. IRC stressed that immediate investment in local economies and livelihood support is critical in the early recovery window to prevent the disaster from deepening the pre-existing humanitarian crisis, given the workforce gaps created by prior mass emigration.

Reporting is frequent and multi-sourced (OCHA, PAHO/WHO, UNDP, UNHCR, UNICEF, UNFPA, IFRC, ACAPS, REACH, UNDRR, NGOs) spanning day +0 to +48, allowing a fairly detailed timeline, but casualty and damage figures are explicitly described by multiple agencies as preliminary and subject to change, with notable discrepancies between sources reporting on the same or similar dates (e.g., 589 vs 920 dead on 26 June; 1,423 vs 2,501 vs 1,500 vs 856 damaged structures across different sitreps). Figures for missing persons remain ambiguous and unreconciled (IFRC), and later UNICEF/CESVI death tolls (4,490-5,208 by mid-to-late July) are not cross-confirmed by PAHO, which continued citing the 3,342-3,300+ figure as of 10 July. No information is provided on pre-event early warning system performance, detailed prevention/building-code history, or final reconstruction costs, leaving medium-to-low confidence in those areas despite high confidence in response and impact chronology.
